en: Homage to you, O Blessed Tārā, who are bound to the entry of beginners!

Whosoever among human beings, being tormented by grief, fear, suffering, and the like, approach a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) out of a desire for liberation from those [afflictions], or out of conformity with others, or out of faith—they should be directed by that spiritual friend, through various specific examples, toward the mind of awakening (bodhicitta) characterized by compassion shared with all sentient beings; having turned them away from agitation caused by suffering and attachment to pleasure, they should also be turned away from the sphere of inferior views.

And as for agitation: all sentient beings who have entered the six realms of existence are beset by suffering, their minds overwhelmed by the latent impressions of pleasure. It should be made known that they are immersed in the three types of suffering. In this regard, those whose minds do not become serene—due to an inclination toward other philosophical systems (*darśanāntara*) or through indolence—are the inferior ones. Those whose minds do not become serene because of belonging to the lineage (*gotra*) of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas are the middling ones; all such persons should be directed toward the states of inferiority and mediocrity. However, those whose minds arise inclined toward accomplishing the welfare of others should be directed onto the path of the sons of the Perfectly Awakened One (*samyaksaṃbuddha*). But those whose minds turn back [from worldly aims] either spontaneously or through the power of their lineage, possessing minds intent on the upliftment of sentient beings—they alone are truly fortunate. Having thus understood the distinctions of inferior, middling, and superior: those who are inferior should be directed merely toward attendance [upon teachers]; whereas those who are middling and superior should be directed toward having no other teacher and toward the single path (*ekāyana*). Having understood this, a practitioner of the Dharma should bring sentient beings to maturity. Thus, regarding the threefold taking of refuge: the inferior are in the refuge of attendance; the middling and superior are in having no other teacher and in the single path. Having understood this, a practitioner of the Dharma should bring sentient beings to maturity.

Thus, regarding these three kinds of going for refuge: the inferior [refuge] consists in taking refuge in worship; the middling and superior [refuges] consist in having no other teacher and in the single path. How, then, should a householder bodhisattva abide? How should he practice?

When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the householder Ugra: "Excellent, excellent, householder! It is worthy of you that you consider it appropriate to inquire about this matter. Therefore, householder, listen and attend closely and well; I shall speak. As to how a householder bodhisattva should abide in the excellence of conduct through the undertaking of the qualities of training, and how he should practice—"

"So be it, Blessed One," Ugra replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this to him: "In this world, a householder bodhisattva living in a home must go for refuge to the Buddha; he must go for refuge to the Dharma; he must go for refuge to the Saṃgha. Desiring the Dharma, having prostrated with the five limbs or the three limbs, with his upper body draped over one shoulder, his right knee-knuckle touching the ground, or squatting, he should, with joined palms holding flowers, entreat the spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) three times."
Having seen the world tormented by suffering, and desiring to go for refuge in order to pacify the suffering of the world, I have perceived the three refuges as they truly are. (1)

Then, one should generate toward the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) the perception of the Teacher, love for the Teacher, and reverence for the Teacher. Other perceptions should also be generated: the perception of [the teacher] as a physician and the perception of [him] as a hero. One should generate in oneself the perception of being a patient and the perception of being a coward. Toward the instructions, one should have the perception of medicine; toward the practices, the perception of the eradication of disease; toward the instructions, the perception of weapons; and toward the practice of the Dharma, the perception of the eradication of the enemies that are the afflictions (*kleśa*). Thereafter, having worshipped Śākyamuni—who stands at the center of the wheel of Dharma—by means of a mandala and the fivefold offering (*pañcopacāra*), and having prostrated with three handfuls of flowers, one should supplicate for self-consecration: "Through your consecration, may I become a Buddha like you and turn the wheel of Dharma. Then, having arranged the mandala for the Buddhas and others and worshipped them with the fivefold offering, one should go for refuge by repeating what has been taught. In this regard, the procedure for the dedication of the mandala and so forth is applied respectively to those who are inferior, middling, and superior.
The mother of sovereignty and health, the increaser of strength and nourishment, the generator of intuitive insight, she who always perfectly grants all accomplishments. (2)

Since this is the worship of the Teacher of the World, it should therefore be performed with diligent effort at the three times of day for the Supreme Lord, the fully awakened Teacher of the World. (3)
I shall describe its ritual procedure correctly and in due order,
as if recollecting and experiencing birth, disease, old age, and death.
On the eighth, the fourteenth, and always on the full moon day, the eightfold fast (upoṣadha) must always be observed with diligent effort. (5)
To him whose body is adorned with the marks of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa),
I perform this maṇḍala out of devotion for the sake of attaining absolute liberation (kaivalya).

At the time of sweeping, the following verses beginning with "The gift of cow dung... should be recited. When constructing the maṇḍala of the Dharma-saṃgha, one should perform the glorification of its virtues: "By whom thirsty beings have been satisfied through the Dharma—to him I offer this water-pot from my heart for the sake of attaining absolute liberation. (7)
Regarding the offering of a water-clock.
With devotion, I offer this priceless *argha*, white as a pearl, for the sake of purification, to the Teacher of the world, who possesses all virtues and is the enemy of the afflictions. (8)
In the offering of the *argha* water.
This is your supreme flower, both aquatic and terrestrial;
I offer it with supreme devotion—accept it as you please. (9)
Having sacrificed hundreds of lives by which awakening was attained, I offer this flower for the sake of nirvāṇa to the one who acts for the benefit of others. (10)
In the offering of flowers.
May this incense be approved for that God of Gods, whose thousands of stupas are worshipped by gods and humans. (11)
Regarding the offering of incense.
With devotion, I offer this gift of a lamp to the Knower of All, by whose temple lamp the darkness of ignorance was destroyed. (12)
Regarding the offering of a lamp.
One should offer a profuse anointing to the Victor with beautiful [ointments] such as full-moon sandalwood and with a sprinkling of saffron water. ||13||
I anoint them with the finest perfumes, whose scents spread throughout all the three-thousandfold world systems;
[with] gold that is refined, polished, and well-washed with lime.
The bodies of all the lords of sages are brilliantly radiant. ||14||
In the offering of anointing substances.
I offer this food-oblation, complete with all its components and provided with various kinds of hard and soft foods, endowed with excellent color, fragrance, and taste; please accept it. (15)
One who offers a lamp becomes pleasing to behold, worthy of worship with a circle of flowers, and attains divine vision. (16)
By offering incense and perfumes, one shall obtain divine fragrances;
by offering food offerings (naivedya), one obtains objects of enjoyment; and by giving clothing, one obtains a beautiful complexion. (17)
By bowing down, one is always born into an exalted family;
by reciting hymns of praise, a person becomes one whose words are always accepted. (18)
By circumambulating [it] clockwise, one becomes wise and possessed of mindfulness at all times;
he who performs this for the sake of liberation will attain liberation in the end. (19)

Thus, that Blessed One—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One—[I offer this mandala] to that Buddha, the Blessed One Śākyamuni. The Dharma, by name, is peaceful, supreme among dispassions, leading to parinirvāṇa, and proclaimed by the Sugata; [I offer this mandala] to that Dharma.

In the Saṅgha there are those practicing for the fruit of stream-entry and those who have attained stream-entry; in the Saṅgha there are those practicing for the fruit of once-returning and those who have attained once-returning; in the Saṅgha there are those practicing for the fruit of non-returning and those who have attained non-returning; in the Saṅgha there are those practicing for the fruit of arhatship and those who have attained arhatship. Venerable sirs, this community of disciples of the Blessed One is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of salutation with joined palms, worthy of respectful service, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world, and worthy of gifts. To that noble Saṅgha, I offer this mandala. In this same way, flowers and other items are also to be offered.
Having conquered the deceitful Māra by that means and attained supreme Buddhahood, may I become a refuge for all embodied beings who are weary of cyclic existence. 20.
As long as I wander through existence, may I be born in auspicious states;
may I associate with the virtuous, be wise, and be devoted to the welfare of the world. (21)

Thus one should make this vow: "Venerable Sir, I, a lay follower (*upāsaka*), go for refuge to the Buddha, the foremost of bipeds, for as long as life lasts, until the end of my life. I go for refuge to the Dharma—the qualities such as the knowledge of exhaustion (*akṣayajñāna*) which constitute the state of a non-learner (*aśaikṣa*) and effect Buddhahood—for the sake of protection from suffering, accepting it as my support. [I go for refuge] to the Buddha, the foremost of bipeds, because he is endowed with virtues characterized by the perfection of his own and others' welfare, and is thus distinguished above all sentient beings. For as long as life lasts, I go for refuge to the Dharma, the best among those free from passion (*virāga*). The Dharma is Nirvana, the foremost among those free from passion. It is the best because, compared to the passions attained through the worldly path, it cannot be lost due to the attainment of the untainted (*anāsrava*) path, and because it is wholesome and eternal. For as long as life lasts, I go for refuge to the Saṃgha, the foremost of assemblies. The Saṃgha consists of the qualities that constitute the community of learners (*śaikṣa*) and non-learners. It is the most excellent of all assemblies of renunciants because it is indivisible and is the unsurpassed field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). It should be understood that by this, one does not obtain the restraint (*saṃvara*) without the intention for Nirvana (*nirvāṇāśaya*), and that the intention for Nirvana does not exist without going for refuge.

For instance: by saying "I go for refuge to the Buddha," one relies upon the teacher of the path to Nirvana; by saying "I go for refuge to the Dharma," because it is the supreme Dharma, one relies upon Nirvana itself; and by saying "I go for refuge to the Saṅgha," one relies upon companions who travel toward the city of Nirvana. This is how it should be understood.

An upāsaka is so called because of his worship of the Three Jewels, his worship of wholesome qualities, and his preservation of the training rules as they have been prescribed. A second time also, I, as an upāsaka, go for refuge to the Buddha for as long as life lasts; I go for refuge to the Dharma for as long as life lasts; I go for refuge to the Saṅgha for as long as life lasts.

A third time also, as a lay follower (*upāsaka*), I go for refuge to the Buddha for as long as life lasts; I go for refuge to the Dharma for as long as life lasts; I go for refuge to the Saṅgha for as long as life lasts. Having gone for refuge to the Buddha, having gone for refuge to the Dharma, and having gone for refuge to the Saṅgha—I, having become a lay follower who has gone for refuge in the Three Jewels, from this moment until morning, in the interval between now and then, shall neither kill a living being nor take what belongs to another.
I shall practice celibacy; I shall avoid false speech;
and I shall by no means go near intoxicants, which are the abode of negligence. (23)
I shall avoid dancing, singing, and ornaments, as well as [the use of] shoes; likewise, high beds, luxurious beds, and eating at all three times of the day. (24)
Thus, following the example of the Arhats, I shall maintain the pure eightfold Poṣadha observance exactly as it was taught by the Buddha. (25)
Having conquered the deceitful Māra by that [means] and attained supreme Buddhahood, may I become a refuge for all embodied beings who are weary of cyclic existence. (26)
As long as I wander through existence, may I be born in happy realms;
may I associate with the virtuous, be wise, and delight in the welfare of the world. (27)

In the center of the Buddha-maṇḍala is Akṣobhya; in the directions starting from the east, Vairocana and the others are situated in their respective order. In the center of the Dharma-maṇḍala is Prajñāpāramitā; in their respective order are the Daśabhūmika, Candrapradīpa, Laṅkāvatāra, and Gaṇḍavyūha. In the center of the Saṃgha-maṇḍala is Lokeśvara; in their respective order are Maitreya, Gaganagañja, Samantabhadra, Vajrapāṇi, Mañjughoṣa, Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin, Kṣitigarbha, and Jñānottara.

Their mantras are as follows: Oṃ hrīḥ lokeśvarāya svāhā | Oṃ maṃ (maiṃ) maitreyāya svāhā | Oṃ gaṃ gaganagañjāya svāhā | Oṃ saṃ samantabhadrāya svāhā | Oṃ yaṃ yakṣādhipataye svāhā | Oṃ maṃ mañjughoṣāya svāhā | Oṃ skaṃ viṣkambhiṇe svāhā | Oṃ kṣiṃ kṣitigarbhāya svāhā | Oṃ jñaṃ jñānottarāya svāhā |

"From this day forward, until I reach the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), I, [name], taking this moment as my starting point, go for refuge to the Buddha, the Blessed One, the Teacher, the Guide, the foremost of bipeds. Thus a second and a third time. As before, I go for refuge to the Dharma, the supreme among those things free from passion. Thus a second and a third time. Likewise, I go for refuge to the Saṅgha of irreversible Bodhisattvas, the best of assemblies. Thus a second and a third time. In that regard, for one who is correctly applied, there is the state of having no other teacher: "From this day forth, the Buddha is my teacher; there are no other teachers. Thus a third time.

But for another, the refuge common to the Saṅgha should be granted for as long as life lasts. Afterwards, he makes himself aware of the Buddhas and the Noble Ones as witnesses: "From this day forth, may the Noble Ones hold me and acknowledge me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge. This is repeated three times.

Then, this root of virtue should be dedicated toward unexcelled perfect enlightenment by means of the dedication to omniscience, as expressed in the passage beginning with "just as... and so forth. Likewise, there is the manifestation of the qualities of the refuge, starting with:
"Many go for refuge to mountains and forests," and so on. After that—
Today my birth has become fruitful; a human existence has been well-attained.
Today I am born into the family of the Buddha; I am now a son of the Buddha. (29)

Then, he should perform worship of the Guru with single-minded devotion to the Three Jewels and instruct him in the Single Path (*ekāyanam*). One who has thus entered [the path] should train as follows: upon seeing the Buddha, the Blessed One, he generates the thought, "I too shall bring to perfection the Buddha-body, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man. Thus he trains. He exerts vigor for the sake of accomplishing those roots of merit by which the thirty-two marks of a Great Man are fully realized. In this way, householder, a lay bodhisattva has gone for refuge to the Buddha. And how, householder, does a lay bodhisattva go for refuge to the Dharma? Here, householder, a lay bodhisattva who has gone for refuge to the Dharma is one who respects the Dharma, who takes the Dharma as his path, who delights in passion for the Dharma, who is inclined toward the Dharma, who is intent on the Dharma, who protects the Dharma, who stands firm in the guardianship of the Dharma, who is bound by the Dharma, who abides in the practice of the Dharma, who seeks the Dharma, whose strength is the Dharma, whose weapon is the Dharma, and who performs the duties of the Dharma. Endowed with such qualities of the Dharma, he attains mindfulness, thinking: "Having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I shall make a righteous distribution of the Dharma to the world of gods, humans, and asuras. In this way, householder, a lay bodhisattva has gone for refuge to the Dharma. And how...

"Householder, a householder bodhisattva has gone for refuge to the Saṅgha. In this regard, householder, when a householder bodhisattva who has gone for refuge to the Saṅgha sees a monk—whether a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat; whether one belonging to the vehicle of the disciples (śrāvakayāna) or the Great Vehicle (mahāyāna)—he regards him with reverence and respect. He rises from his seat in honor of the teacher, is easy to speak to, and is receptive to instruction. Toward those who have gone rightly and practice rightly, even while remaining seated, he attains such mindfulness: 'Once I too have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I shall teach the Dharma for the sake of accomplishing the qualities of a disciple and for the sake of accomplishing the qualities of a solitary buddha. Thus he is reverent and respectful toward them, yet he does not covet anything from them."

"In this way, householder, a lay bodhisattva has gone for refuge to the Saṅgha. Furthermore, householder, a lay bodhisattva endowed with four qualities has gone for refuge to the Buddha. Which four? By not abandoning the thought of awakening (bodhicitta); by not breaking one's formal undertaking; by not forsaking great compassion (mahākaruṇā); and by not taking other [objects] as a basis for one's abiding. Householder, a lay bodhisattva endowed with these four qualities has gone for refuge to the Buddha. Householder, a lay bodhisattva endowed with four qualities has gone for refuge to the Dharma. Which four? By serving, attending upon, and associating with persons who speak the Dharma; by listening to the Dharma with due respect; by examining it thoroughly and fundamentally after having heard the Dharma; and by teaching and elucidating to others the teachings one has fully mastered exactly as they were heard. By dedicating the roots of virtue born from that gift of Dharma toward unexcelled perfect awakening (anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi). Householder, a lay bodhisattva endowed with these four qualities has gone for refuge to the Dharma."

Furthermore, householder, a lay bodhisattva endowed with four qualities has gone for refuge to the Saṅgha. What are these four? He transforms the mind of omniscience in those followers of the Śrāvaka vehicle who have not yet entered the fixed course of rightness; he gathers them in and unites them with the Dharma through that gathering; he takes refuge in the Saṅgha of irreversible bodhisattvas and does not take refuge in the Saṅgha of Śrāvakas; and he does not incline toward the qualities or the conduct of the Śrāvakas, nor does he develop an inclination for those qualities. Householder, a lay bodhisattva endowed with these four qualities has gone for refuge to the Saṅgha.

The refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and so forth, which was proclaimed by the Victor as the gateway [to liberation], should therefore be taken; for even the wholesome dharma does not arise otherwise. (30)
Those beings who, having taken no refuge, have made a firm resolve for enlightenment, never reach their limit, just as those with a damaged ship do not reach the end of the ocean. //31//
The sequence for taking possession of the ground and so forth during the worship of the Guru and others is as before;
the distinction here, however, is that the mandala itself is circular.
In the center of that, one should visualize Mount Meru, arising from the syllable *HŪṂ*, adorned with eight peaks, divine, consisting of the four jewels, square, and most beautiful. ||33||
Adorned in the east and other directions with silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, and gold, it has golden pillars below and is embellished with continents and sub-continents. ||34||

The eastern continent of Pūrvavideha is white like a half-moon and originates from the syllable *yaṃ*; it is flanked on both sides by the syllables *yā* and *jā*, representing Deha and Uttarakuru respectively. ||35||
One should place Jambūdvīpa, which is triangular, in the south, arising from the syllable *raṃ*;
it is surrounded on its sides by the two islands of Rāja and Śāṭha-mantrin. (36)
One should place the circular Godānīya island, born from the syllable *vaṃ*, to the west, surrounded by the two islands of Amaravara and Vāyu. ||37||
One should meditate on the continent of Uttarakuru as square and moving, surrounded on both sides by the Kurus and Kauravas, and by the Lā and Jā [mountains]. (38)
Having meditated upon the locations with diamonds, sapphire, lapis lazuli, emerald, lotus-stone, and agate, as well as gold, pearls, coral, and so forth, one should fill them. (39)

And on the periphery, there are circles of men and women in the cardinal directions with rows of *ra* and *la*; and in the corner regions, there are those produced from *yā*, *yaṃ*, *laṃ*, and *vā*. ||40||
Having completed the full mandala with the sword, the elephant flanks, the jewels, and likewise the eight treasures, together with their seed-syllables and the [deity] bodies.

Having uttered the designations of the locations with flowers accompanied by perfumes and other offerings, one should draw forth what was previously given and join it to those respective locations. 42.
Having established the flowers and the lamps and so forth with their respective mantras, one should offer them to the gurus and the bodhisattvas with a sincere intention. (43)

The praise, the dedication, and the dismissal are as before. One should dismiss with the syllable *mur*. Together with this very [mantra], the wise one should meditate upon the maṇḍala of the True Dharma and the maṇḍala of the service to the Guru and others—the maṇḍala of the True Dharma as Mount Meru together with the four continents, filled with various kinds of jewels—and thus perform the rite. (44)
One should worship with excellent flowers according to their respective places, using the seed-syllables and names;
having offered [the gift] to the Dharma whose nature is all-pervading, one should recite the composed Dharma-text. (45)

Having reflected upon the welfare of sentient beings, the long endurance of the teaching, and the arousal [of virtue], one who is compassionate by nature should move about with a mind of loving-kindness. (46)

May all beings, all living creatures, and all spirits without exception—may they all indeed be happy; may they all be free from disease; may they all behold auspicious things; and may no one encounter evil. (47)
May the teaching—the sole medicine for the suffering of the world, the source of all prosperity and happiness—endure for a long time, accompanied by gain and honor. (48)
The long endurance of the teaching.
From that single support, clouds of Buddhas and their sons—beings equal to oneself, arisen from infinite fields—issue forth. (49)
Thinking, "May they attain purity for the body of Mañjubhadra," the compassionate one should recite the King of Vidyās eight times. (50)

Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas! Homage be to you, O Great Hero, who brings benefit to all sentient beings! Abide everywhere, having empowered all phenomena! Svāhā! This is the dwelling in loving-kindness (*maitrīvihāra*). This too is connected to the entry into the preliminary practices (*ādikarmāvatāra*). The extent of this text is one hundred and ten verses.
